subtype: Approach: scenario planning for power and phone loss [Thinking]
passage:
Gopika: Okay, imagine the cyclone knocks out the towers and the power. Two days, no phone. What do we do?
Irawati: Charge everything tonight?
Gopika: A power bank helps, but say it dies too. Then what?
Irawati: Then... I only know my brother's number by heart, and that's because it never changed.
Gopika: So we write numbers on paper. Warden, both our families, the ward office, the clinic. Tape the list inside the cupboard door.
Irawati: The caretaker has a small radio. I'll ask if we can borrow it.
Gopika: Good. And we download an offline map of the way to the school shelter tonight.
Irawati: Who calls whom?
Gopika: Whoever finds signal first calls your brother in Nagpur, and he tells everyone else. One person outside the city.
Irawati: Fine, I'll warn him now. Nothing fancy, just what the phones can't do.

qa.q: Where will the paper list of numbers be kept?
qa.a: The list will be taped inside the cupboard door.

qa.q: What does Irawati's remark about knowing only one number by heart suggest about how Irawati feels?
qa.a: It suggests Irawati feels a little uneasy and exposed, since the phone holds nearly all the contacts.

qa.q: What else could Gopika and Irawati agree on, and why?
qa.a: They could agree a fixed meeting point in case the hostel is unsafe, because without phones they cannot message each other to find one another.

qa.q: How might Irawati's brother in Nagpur see his part in the plan?
qa.a: He would probably feel responsible and a little anxious, since he is the one outside contact who passes messages to everyone.

grounding: Illustrates imagining two days without power and phones and planning a paper list, a radio or offline map, and who contacts whom.

subtype: Approach: scenario planning for power and phone loss [Thinking]
passage:
After last year's cyclone knocked out power and phones for a day and a half, I sat down in May and asked myself: what if it happens again, but for two days?
First problem: I don't know anyone's number by heart. So I wrote a paper list, with Mummy, Papa, my uncle in Vizag, our neighbour Pankaj bhaiya, the local police station and the hospital, and put it in a zip bag.
Second: no internet means no maps. I downloaded an offline map of the city and bought a small battery radio for news.
Third: who calls whom? I made a simple chain with the family: if we're separated, everyone tries Papa first. If Papa can't be reached, we try my uncle outside the city, since outside lines might work when ours don't.
We tested it in August. It worked. I'm Tarun, and planning for silence turned out to be half the preparation.

qa.q: Who is everyone meant to try first if separated?
How did Tarun feel about the idea of being cut off again?
qa.a: Tarun was worried enough about being cut off for two days to sit down and plan every gap, likely remembering how uneasy last year felt.

qa.q: What else could Tarun add to the plan?
qa.a: Tarun could add a fixed meeting place in case even the uncle can't be reached, since phones may fail completely.

qa.q: How might Pankaj bhaiya feel being on Tarun's paper list?
qa.a: Pankaj bhaiya might feel trusted and ready to help, knowing the family would reach out in an emergency.

grounding: Shows the person imagining being cut off for two days and planning a paper contact list, a radio and offline map, and a shared plan on who contacts whom.

subtype: Approach: scenario planning for power and phone loss [Thinking]
passage:
Hostel warden's note, May. Written by Jaya.
Akash, a second-year student from the coastal belt, came to the office to share a plan he'd made after last year's storm, when the hostel lost power and phone signal for two days.
He had imagined the same thing happening again and asked, "What would I need if my phone was useless?" His answer was on a single laminated sheet: a paper list of his parents' numbers, the hostel landline, my office extension and the district control room; the location of the nearest relief centre marked on a printed map; and a note that he carries a small battery radio.
He also showed a plan he had agreed with his family: if nobody can reach anyone, his sister calls the hostel landline and Akash calls his uncle in another city.
What I did next: I asked if I could copy his sheet as a template for all residents, and he agreed.

qa.q: What did Akash's laminated sheet include?
qa.a: A paper list of important numbers, the nearest relief centre marked on a printed map, and a note that he carries a battery radio.

qa.q: What worry was behind Akash's plan?
qa.a: He was worried about being cut off again like last year, asking what he would need if his phone was useless.

qa.q: What else could Akash's plan include?
qa.a: It could include a meeting point on the campus in case the hostel itself has to be evacuated.

qa.q: How does the warden see Akash's plan?
qa.a: The warden sees it as useful enough to share with every resident, and asks to copy it as a template.

grounding: Shows a student imagining power and phone loss for two days and planning a paper contact list, a radio, a printed map and a family contact plan.
